meta.blurb: When her mother breaks a wrist in a simple fall, Tess discovers that bones are alive, always rebuilding, and shaped by what we eat and do. Follow one family through a year of learning how to look after the skeleton for life.
meta.bible: Tess: a woman of about forty-two who works in a library and learns about bones after her mother's fall. Joan: Tess's mother, aged seventy-four, practical, funny and stubborn; she breaks her wrist in a fall on a wet garden step in spring. Leo: Tess's son, aged fourteen, tall, sporty and always hungry; he says bones are dead sticks, then learns better. Dr Rahman: Joan's family doctor, calm and clear. Priya: the physiotherapist who leads a balance and strength class at the health centre. The story runs for one year, from one spring to the next. Key terms: Bone, Bones, Skeleton, Collagen, Calcium, Phosphate, Marrow, Remodelling, Osteoporosis, Osteopenia, Menopause, Oestrogen, Fracture, Wrist, Hip, Spine, DXA, Vitamin D, Sunlight, Protein, Sardines, Kale, Tofu, Spinach, Oxalate, Weight-bearing, Resistance, Balance, Tai chi, Steroid, Physiotherapist, Pharmacist. Facts used: bone is living tissue that is constantly broken down and rebuilt; most of the skeleton is built in childhood and the teen years, with peak bone mass in the late twenties or so; bone loss speeds up in women around the menopause and also happens in men; osteoporosis is thin, fragile bone and is usually silent until a break; a DXA scan is a quick, low-dose X-ray scan of the hip and spine; calcium recommendations differ between countries and ages; vitamin D comes from sunlight, a few foods and supplements; bones respond to load, so weight-bearing, impact and strength exercise help; most fractures follow falls, so balance matters; smoking and heavy drinking harm bones; long-term steroid tablets can thin bones and must never be stopped without a doctor. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, clear, practical and hopeful; honest about what is uncertain; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice.

beats.summary: A home check for rugs, poor light, slippery steps and missing handrails helps to prevent falls.

beats.summary: Falls are also reduced by regular eye tests, sensible shoes and reviewing medicines that cause dizziness with a doctor or pharmacist.

B1B2: One spring afternoon, Tess is working at the library when her phone rings. Her mother, Joan, has slipped on a wet garden step and has hurt her wrist badly.
At the hospital, an X-ray shows that Joan's wrist is broken. Dr Rahman explains that a break from such a simple fall is a good reason to check her bones.
That evening Tess realises that she knows almost nothing about bones. Her son Leo, who is fourteen, shrugs and says they are just dead sticks that hold us up.
Tess reads that bone is a living tissue, with blood vessels, nerves and cells inside it. It grows, it heals and it changes, just like skin or muscle.
A bone has a hard, smooth shell on the outside. Inside, the bone is more like a honeycomb, and in the middle of many bones there is soft marrow.
Bone is made of two main ingredients, and each one has a job to do. Collagen is a tough, flexible protein, and minerals such as calcium make it hard, a little like steel rods in concrete.
All through life, the body removes tiny pieces of old bone and builds new bone in their place. This steady renewal is called remodelling, and it never stops.
One team of cells removes old bone, and another team builds new bone. As long as the two teams stay in balance, the bones remain strong.
Most of the skeleton is built during childhood and the teenage years. Some scientists describe this as paying money into a bone bank for later life.
Leo has grown several centimetres this year, and his bones have been working hard to keep up. Most people reach their peak bone mass in their late twenties or so.
After the peak, most people lose a little bone every year, slowly at first. A strong start and good habits both help, because they leave more bone in the bank.
Joan remembers the menopause, when her periods stopped in her early fifties. The hormone oestrogen helps to protect bone, and when it falls, bone loss speeds up for some years.
Men lose bone as they age as well, though usually later and more slowly. Osteoporosis is less common in men than in women, but it is not rare.
The word osteoporosis means porous bone, or bone full of small holes. The holes inside the bones become larger, so the bones are thinner and weaker and break more easily.
The worrying thing about thinning bones is that they usually do not hurt. Most people have no warning at all until a bone breaks.
Thin bones most often break in the wrist, the hip and the spine. Sometimes the small bones of the spine collapse, so a person slowly becomes shorter and more bent.
Dr Rahman arranges a special DXA scan of the bones for Joan. It is a quick, painless, low-dose X-ray of the hip and spine, and it measures how dense the bones are.
Some things that raise the risk of weak bones cannot be changed, such as age or a parent who broke a hip. Others, such as smoking or never exercising, can be changed.
The scan shows some thinning in Joan's bones, and Dr Rahman explains the options kindly. There are medicines that can lower the risk of breaks, and the choice belongs to Joan and her doctor.
That night Tess cannot sleep, so she keeps reading. The good news is that bone responds to how we eat and how we move, at every age.
Calcium is the main mineral in bone, and nearly all of the body's calcium is stored in the bones and teeth. We cannot make it, so it has to come from food.
Milk, yoghurt and cheese are all rich in calcium. So are fortified plant milks, tinned sardines with soft bones, kale, broccoli and tofu made with calcium.
Many people think that spinach is a great source of calcium. It does contain some, but it also has oxalate, which stops the body from using most of it.
Health organisations do not all agree on how much calcium to eat each day. The advice differs between countries and between age groups, so any figure is only a rough guide.
Most experts say that food is the best way to get calcium. Large doses of calcium tablets are not always helpful, so people should ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking them.
Vitamin D helps the gut to take in calcium, so bones need it too. The skin makes vitamin D when sunlight falls on it.
How much vitamin D the skin makes depends on the season, where you live and how much time you spend outdoors. Darker skin makes it more slowly, and burning in the sun is never the goal.
Only a few foods have much vitamin D, mainly oily fish, egg yolks and some fortified foods. In many countries, health bodies advise supplements for some groups, especially in winter.
The framework of bone is made of protein, so eating enough protein matters too. Beans, eggs, fish, meat and dairy foods all provide it, and many older people do not eat enough.
Leo needs plenty of good food because his bones are growing so fast. Very strict diets in the teenage years can harm bones, and Tess makes sure that he eats well.
Bones grow stronger when they are used, but weaker when they are not. Astronauts in space lose bone because their skeletons carry no weight, so they must exercise for about two hours every day.
Walking, dancing, hiking and climbing stairs all make the bones work against gravity. Swimming and cycling are excellent for the heart, but they put less load on the bones.
Short bursts of impact, like jumping or skipping, seem to build bone, especially in young people. Some studies of schoolchildren found gains from only a few minutes of jumping a day.
Strength training with weights or stretchy bands also helps. When muscles pull hard on the bones, the bones respond by growing a little stronger.
Joan meets Priya, a physiotherapist, who tells her to start gently. People with thin bones should get advice before they try deep forward bends, heavy twists or high impact.
Tess and Joan begin walking together every morning, and they take the stairs wherever they can. Leo joins them with a skipping rope, and the whole family laughs about it.
Priya reminds them that most broken bones follow a fall. Strong bones help, but preventing the fall in the first place matters just as much.
Priya teaches Joan to practise balance, beginning with standing on one leg beside a kitchen counter. Classes such as tai chi can also help to reduce the risk of falls.
Tess walks around her mother's house and garden looking for hazards. She finds a curling rug, a dim stair light and the slippery step where Joan fell.
Falls are also less likely if you have regular eye tests and wear sturdy, well-fitting shoes. A pharmacist or doctor can check whether any medicine causes dizziness.
Smoking is bad for bones, and so is regular heavy drinking. Joan's neighbour has just given up cigarettes, and Joan tells him how pleased she is.
Some medicines, such as steroid tablets taken for many months, can thin the bones. Doctors weigh this against the benefits, and nobody should stop a medicine on their own.
People who are very underweight are more likely to have thin bones, and eating disorders can do serious harm to the skeleton. Anyone who is worried about their eating should ask a doctor for help.
After about six weeks, the cast comes off Joan's wrist, and the bone has healed. Tess thinks that this is the best proof of all that bone is alive.
For a school project, Leo makes a poster about bones and presents it to his class. He begins with the words, Bones are not dead sticks, and Tess smiles from the back.
Joan goes back to see Dr Rahman to talk about her plan. He tells her that scans are not repeated often, because bones change slowly.
When winter comes, Dr Rahman advises Joan to take a vitamin D supplement. In many cold and dark places, doctors give this advice to older adults.
One year later, spring has come round again, and Joan walks across the garden steps with ease. She goes to Priya's class every week and has not fallen once since.
Tess writes a plan for every age and sticks it to the fridge. Children should eat well and jump about, adults should lift and walk, and older people should add balance practice.
This book gives general information about bones, and it is not medical advice. Anyone with a fracture, a health condition or a worry about their bones should ask a doctor.
C1C2: One spring afternoon, Tess was stacking returned books at the library when her phone began to buzz insistently in her pocket. It was a neighbour, calling to say that her mother Joan had slipped on a wet garden step and was now sitting in the kitchen, unusually pale, cradling her wrist. Tess abandoned the trolley where it stood, apologised to her startled colleagues and ran for her car with her keys already in her hand.

At the hospital, the X-ray glowed on the screen, and it showed a clean break just above the wrist. Dr Rahman, a calm man with a gift for plain speech, explained that a bone which breaks in a fall from standing height can be a sign that the bones have grown thinner. It did not mean anything was certain, he added, only that it was sensible to look into it.

That evening, over a late dinner, Tess admitted to herself that she knew almost nothing about the hundreds of structures holding her upright. Leo, who was fourteen and permanently hungry, shrugged and declared that bones were just dead sticks that held you up, like the poles of a tent. Tess, a librarian by trade and by instinct, decided that this particular question would be answered properly.

The first thing Tess discovered in the library's science shelves was that Leo was wrong. Bone is a living tissue, threaded with blood vessels and nerves and crowded with busy cells, and it grows, repairs itself and responds to its surroundings in much the same way as skin or muscle. A skeleton on a classroom stand is a very different thing from a skeleton in a living person.

Tess learned that a bone is built like a very clever piece of engineering, with a dense, hard shell on the outside and a lighter, spongy lattice within. The lattice resembles a honeycomb, which makes the bone strong without making it heavy, and in the centre of many bones lies the soft marrow, where blood cells are made. Nature, it seemed, had been solving problems of strength and weight for millions of years.

Bone, Tess read, owes all of its remarkable properties to a close partnership between two quite different ingredients. Collagen, a tough and slightly flexible protein, forms a framework, and minerals such as calcium and phosphate harden it, rather in the way that steel rods and concrete work together in a building. Concrete alone would crack and steel alone would bend, but combined they resist both.

Even in an adult, the skeleton is never finished, because the body is constantly removing tiny pieces of old bone and replacing them with new. This process, which scientists call remodelling, is so steady that much of the adult skeleton is renewed over a period of years, though the exact speed differs from one bone to another. Tess found it astonishing that something so solid could be so quietly in motion.

Tess pictured two crews working side by side on the same building, one demolishing worn sections and the other laying fresh bricks. One kind of cell removes old bone, another builds new bone, and as long as the two crews stay in balance the skeleton remains sturdy. When the demolition outpaces the building, however, the bones slowly grow thinner, and that is how a sturdy skeleton can become a fragile one.

Most of a person's skeleton is laid down during childhood and the teenage years, and the bones of the young grow longer, wider and denser at a remarkable pace. Some scientists compare this period to making deposits in a bank account, since the stronger the bones are at the end of it, the more there is to draw on later. Every jump from a garden wall, it turns out, is a small investment in the future, and every skipped meal a small withdrawal.

Leo had grown several centimetres in a single year, and Tess marked his height on the doorframe with a mixture of pride and alarm. All that growth requires a great deal of raw material, and the teenage years are an especially important time for bones, since peak bone mass is usually reached in the late twenties or thereabouts. After that point the aim is to keep as much of it as possible.

After the peak, bone is generally lost very slowly, a little each year, rather as a bank balance shrinks when more is withdrawn than deposited. The rate differs from person to person and depends on inherited traits, diet, activity and health, which is why neither a strong start nor good habits later can be treated as the whole story. Both, Tess noted with some relief, are within reach of nearly everyone, whatever their age, and neither has to be perfect to be of use.

Joan, who had been through the menopause more than twenty years earlier, listened with the attention of a woman hearing her own story told by a stranger. The hormone oestrogen helps to protect bone, Tess explained, so when its level falls the loss of bone speeds up for several years, which is one reason why thinning bones are more common in women. It was, Joan said, the first time anyone had explained it without a sigh.

It would be a mistake to think that thinning bones are only a problem for women, Tess discovered, because men lose bone as they age too. The process generally begins later and proceeds more gradually, and osteoporosis is less common in men, but it is far from rare and is often discovered only after a fracture. Tess made a note to mention it to the men in her family, who had never once been asked about their bones.

The word osteoporosis comes from Greek words meaning porous bone, and it describes bones whose internal lattice has become thin and open. Such bones are less dense and more fragile, so a minor fall, or even a cough or a sharp bend, may be enough to break one. Tess realised that this was precisely what Dr Rahman had been gently pointing at in the hospital.

What worried Tess most was that thinning bones give almost no warning, because they cannot be felt and rarely cause any pain. For many people the first sign is a fracture, and a large number of those who have osteoporosis never learn about it until something snaps. Silence, she thought, is the most dangerous feature of an ailment that is otherwise so manageable.

Fractures caused by thin bones most commonly occur in the wrist, the hip and the bones of the spine. Small breaks in the spine are sometimes unnoticed, and over the years they can make a person gradually shorter and more stooped, so a noticeable loss of height is worth mentioning to a doctor. A broken hip, by contrast, is a serious event that often changes a person's independence.

Dr Rahman arranged a DXA scan for Joan, and she lay on a narrow table while a flat arm passed slowly above her hips and lower back. The scan is a quick, painless, low-dose X-ray that measures the density of the bones, and it was over so rapidly that Joan thought it had not yet begun. Doctors usually combine the result with other facts, such as age and family history, to judge the risk of a break.

Tess drew two columns on a notepad, one for the risks she could change and one for those she could not. Age, a family history of broken hips, a small frame and some long-term illnesses fell into the first column, while smoking, heavy drinking, inactivity and a poor diet fell into the second. The shorter first column, she realised, was no reason to ignore the longer second.

The scan showed some thinning of Joan's bones, and Dr Rahman explained the findings carefully, without alarm and without any hurry. Medicines exist which can reduce the risk of further breaks in people who need them, he said, and the decision about them belongs to the patient and the doctor together, after talking through the benefits and the downsides. Joan, who had always disliked taking tablets and distrusted anything with a long name, asked for a little time to think it over.

That night Tess lay awake worrying about her mother, and then, since sleep refused to come, she reached for the book beside her bed. It brought one fact that eased her mind, namely that living bone responds to the way in which it is treated, and that food, movement and daily habits can all make a real difference at any age. Nothing could be done about her mother's past, but there was a great deal to be done about the future.

Calcium is the chief mineral in bone, and nearly all of the calcium in the human body is stored in the bones and teeth. The body cannot manufacture it, so a steady supply must come from food, and when the diet falls short the body will quietly borrow from the skeleton to keep its other systems running. Bones, in effect, serve as the body's emergency pantry, which is useful in a crisis and unfortunate if it is raided too often.

Tess made a list of the foods that carry calcium, and she was surprised by how varied it was. Milk, yoghurt and cheese are the best-known sources, but fortified plant milks, tinned sardines eaten with their soft bones, kale, broccoli and tofu set with calcium all contribute generously. A balanced diet, she saw, gives most people a good deal of what they need without any special effort.

Tess had always believed that spinach was a champion source of calcium, and she was a little disappointed to learn otherwise. It does contain the mineral, but it also contains oxalate, a natural substance that binds to calcium in the gut and stops most of it from being absorbed. Spinach remains a healthy food, she concluded, but it should not be counted on for bones.

When Tess compared the advice from different health organisations, she found that they did not agree on a single figure. Recommended daily amounts of calcium differ from country to country and from one age group to another, and in general they range from roughly seven hundred to twelve hundred milligrams for adults. A doctor or dietitian, she noted, can say what is sensible for a particular person.

In general, experts prefer that people obtain their calcium from food, where it arrives along with protein and other useful nutrients. Large doses of calcium tablets are not clearly better and can occasionally cause side effects, so anyone thinking of taking them should first talk to a doctor or a pharmacist. Joan, pouring herself a cup of tea, observed that this at least was an excuse for more cheese.

Calcium on its own is not enough, Tess learned, because the body also needs vitamin D to absorb it properly from the food in the gut. Remarkably, the skin can make this vitamin for itself when sunlight falls on it, which is why it is sometimes called the sunshine vitamin. Without enough of it, bones can become soft and weak even when the diet is full of calcium.

The amount of vitamin D that the skin can make depends on the season, the latitude, the colour of the skin and the time spent outdoors. In countries far from the equator the winter sun is too weak for the skin to make much, and people with darker skin generally need more time in the sun to make the same amount. Short, sensible exposure is enough, since sunburn is a danger that no vitamin can excuse.

Surprisingly few foods contain much vitamin D, and oily fish, egg yolks and fortified products such as certain cereals and spreads are the main ones. For this reason many health authorities recommend a supplement for certain groups, such as older adults, people who seldom go outdoors and, in some northern countries, nearly everyone during the darker months. Dr Rahman, Tess noted, would be the right person to advise Joan on that question, since no book could know her circumstances.

The framework of bone is built from the protein collagen, so a diet which lacks protein can undermine bone and muscle together. Beans, lentils, eggs, fish, meat, dairy products and tofu all supply it, and many older people, whose appetites fade and whose meals shrink, do not eat as much as their bodies need. Joan, whose breakfast had long consisted of a single piece of dry toast, took the point with good grace.

Leo, with the insatiable appetite of a boy in the middle of a growth spurt, was easy to feed but not always easy to feed well. Growing bones need a generous supply of energy and nutrients, and very strict dieting in the teenage years can interfere with building a strong skeleton, which is a loss that is difficult to recover later. Tess started cooking breakfast every morning and, to her surprise, Leo ate it all.

Tess found proof that bones respond to the demands placed on them in an unlikely place, namely in space. Astronauts living in weightlessness lose bone because their skeletons are no longer carrying the body's weight, and they therefore spend about two hours of each day exercising in order to protect it. Bone, it seemed, is a thrifty tissue that keeps only what it has reason to keep.

Exercise that makes the body work against gravity, such as walking, dancing, hiking and climbing stairs, gives the bones a useful challenge. Swimming and cycling are wonderful for the heart and lungs and gentle on the joints, but because the water or the saddle carries the weight, they place much less load on the skeleton. Tess suggested a daily walk, and Joan agreed on the condition that it include a café.

Activities that involve a little impact, such as skipping, jumping and running, appear to be especially good at stimulating bone growth in the young. Some studies in schools have found measurable gains in children who did only a few minutes of jumping several times a week, though the results are modest and vary from study to study. Leo, who had always been told to stop jumping on the sofa, felt suddenly vindicated.

Lifting weights or pulling against elastic bands may sound like an activity for athletes, yet it is among the most useful things that anyone can do for the skeleton. Strong muscles pull on the bones that they attach to, and that tension seems to encourage the bones to hold on to their strength, while the muscles themselves also help to prevent falls. Progress should be gradual, Tess read, and a trained instructor can show good technique.

Joan's doctor sent her to Priya, a physiotherapist with a brisk manner and a very warm smile, who showed her how to begin exercising safely. People with thinning bones should seek advice before attempting deep forward bends, forceful twists or jumping, Priya explained, because some movements put more stress on the spine than others. Joan was relieved to hear that there was plenty she could do and that it did not involve a gym.

Within a week the family had turned small habits into a quiet programme of exercise, with a daily walk, stairs instead of lifts and a skipping rope that Leo had found at the back of a cupboard. None of it required a membership or a special outfit, and all of it required the bones to carry weight, which, Tess reminded herself, was exactly the point. Joan, who had expected to resent it, found that she looked forward to the morning.

Most fractures in older people follow a fall, Priya reminded them, so strengthening the skeleton is only half of the plan, and preventing the fall is at least as important. It is a point that is easily overlooked when the conversation centres on diet and medicine, though it may be the most practical advice of all. Tess looked at her mother's bandaged wrist and understood the point at once, as one understands a lesson learned the hard way.

Balance, Priya explained, is a skill that fades if it is not practised, but it can be trained at any age. She showed Joan how to stand on one leg beside the kitchen counter, with a hand close by for safety, and recommended gentle classes such as tai chi, which research suggests can lower the risk of falling. Joan practised every morning while the kettle boiled, wobbling at first and then steadier, like a heron in a cardigan.

Armed with a notebook, Tess walked around her mother's house and garden looking for anything that might cause a fall. She found a curling rug, a dim light on the stairs, a missing handrail by the back door and the very step, green with moss, on which Joan had slipped. By the end of the weekend the rug was gone, the bulbs were brighter and the step had been scrubbed.

Other risks, Priya said, are quieter but no less real, such as poor eyesight, unsupportive shoes and medicines that cause drowsiness or dizziness. Joan booked an eye test, retired her worn-out slippers and asked a pharmacist to review her tablets, in the confident knowledge that a few small checks could prevent a great deal of grief. No medicine should ever be changed or stopped without advice from a doctor first, Dr Rahman warned, however sensible the change might seem.

Tess learned that smoking and heavy drinking are both harmful to the skeleton, as they are to so many other parts of the body. Smokers tend to have thinner bones and a higher risk of fractures, and regular heavy drinking raises the chance of falls as well as damaging bone directly. When Joan's neighbour announced that he had given up cigarettes after forty years, she cheered him over the fence.

Certain medicines can have an effect on the skeleton, and the best known are steroid tablets taken for months or years, which may thin the bones as a side effect. In such cases the medicine often does important work for the patient, so doctors weigh the benefit against the risk, and no one should ever stop a tablet on their own because of something they have read. Tess underlined this in her notes twice and then, for good measure, drew a small box around it so that she would never forget.

Being very underweight is a risk to the bones, and serious eating disorders can damage them badly, particularly when they begin in the teenage years while the skeleton is still being built. Tess was careful to read this part slowly, because it concerned something that real families sometimes face. Anyone troubled by their eating, she resolved, should be urged to talk to a doctor without delay.

After about six weeks the cast came off Joan's wrist, and the X-ray showed that the broken ends had knitted together into a single bone again. The body had done it without being asked, by sending cells to the site, laying down new material and gradually reshaping it, and Tess found the process more convincing than any textbook. Dead sticks, she reflected with quiet satisfaction, do not mend themselves, and Leo would have to admit it at last.

When Leo's class was asked to prepare a presentation on any part of the human body, he surprised his teacher by choosing bone. He opened with the words, “Bones are not dead sticks,” and went on to talk, with only a few glances at his notes, about collagen, calcium and a family that had learned to look after its skeleton. Tess, standing at the back of the classroom, did not trust herself to say a word.

Joan returned to see Dr Rahman for a review of everything that had happened since the fall, and she was pleased to be able to report that she had stuck to her plan. Bones change slowly, he told her, so scans are usually repeated only after a period of years, and the treatment decision would be revisited in line with how she was and what the evidence showed. He was, she told Tess afterwards in the car, as reassuring as a warm bath, and considerably less likely to go cold.

When the dark months arrived, Dr Rahman advised Joan to take a daily vitamin D supplement, which is something that doctors in many northern countries suggest for older adults and for anyone who rarely goes outdoors. The dose is small and the supplement is inexpensive, Tess noted, but the decision is for each person and their own doctor to make, rather than for a book to make for them. Joan placed the bottle next to the teapot, where she would never overlook it.

A year later the spring came round again, and Joan walked down the garden step, now fitted with a sturdy handrail, with the confidence of someone half her age. She attended Priya's balance class every week, took her daily walk in all weathers and had not fallen once in twelve months. Tess watched from the kitchen window and felt, quite unexpectedly, that she might cry.

Tess wrote out a plan for every age of life and stuck it to the fridge, where all three generations of the family could see it. Children should eat well and jump about, adults should walk, lift and avoid tobacco, and older people should add balance practice and regular check-ups with a doctor, and everybody should get some sunlight and enough calcium and protein. It was not complicated, she thought, only a matter of doing the simple things for long enough.

As the family finished their tea, Tess felt that her bones, her mother's and her son's were at last in good hands, namely their own. This book gives general information only and is not medical advice, so anyone who has broken a bone, who has a health condition or who has a worry about their bones should speak to a doctor. For everyone else, a short walk after supper, with a glass of milk or a piece of fruit to follow, is a perfectly fine place to begin.
